Reading a stack trace

The exit code tells you almost nothing on its own. A SIGSEGV reported as code 139 means the kernel killed the process, and the useful information is the frame the fault came from, not the number the shell printed.

Compile with debug symbols before spending an afternoon guessing. A stripped binary yields addresses; the same binary built with DWARF data yields function names and lines, and the bug usually becomes obvious as soon as it has a name.

Use code from the release tag when reproducing, not from the branch tip. A trace read against the wrong revision points at a line that moved, and the resulting theory is confidently wrong.

ASAN and UBSAN catch entire classes of this before the crash happens. They cost runtime performance in CI and repay it the first time they turn a heisenbug into a deterministic failure.
